text: The question we address in this paper is whether eye and hand can work independently when searching. <sentence_start/>It is well known that eyes and hands often move in a highly coordinated manner. <sentence_start/>This happens in simple tasks such as pointing at objects (Neggers and Bekkering <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR16" doi="10.1152/jn.2000.83.2.639" pmid="10669480" count="1">2000</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR17" doi="10.1016/S0167-9457(02)00120-3" pmid="12381393" count="1">2002</citation>) and drawing ellipses (Reina and Schwartz <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22" doi="10.1016/S0167-9457(02)00156-2" pmid="12667746" count="1">2003</citation>), as well as in more complicated ones such as manipulating blocks (Johansson et al. <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.21-17-06917.2001" pmcid="PMC6763066" pmid="11517279" count="1">2001</citation>) or preparing sandwiches and making tea (Land and Hayhoe <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" doi="10.1016/S0042-6989(01)00102-X" pmid="11718795" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, eyes and hands can also move independently and perform tasks in parallel. <sentence_start/>Boucher et al. (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.3758/bf03193779" pmid="17929700" count="1">2007</citation>) studied participant’s ability to stop eye and hand movements that had already been initiated. <sentence_start/>They found that stopping eye movements and stopping hand movements are not completely dependent but also not completely independent processes. <sentence_start/>Stritzke and Trommershäuser (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR24" doi="10.1016/j.visres.2007.04.013" pmid="17532361" count="1">2007</citation>) found that in a rapid pointing task the eye movements are not anchored to the hand movements, but are instead, like in visual search, driven by low-level visual features.

text: The management of gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB) is one of the most common clinical problems encountered by gastrointestinal endoscopists. <sentence_start/>The type of bleeding, such as upper vs. lower GIB, acute vs. chronic, or overt vs. covert, its accompanying symptoms and laboratory parameters are all used as guidance in deciding how to structure the workup and which endoscopic procedures to choose for GIB workup and its management. [<citation rid="R1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11796865" doi="10.1136/pmj.78.915.4" pmcid="PMC1742226" count="1">1</citation>-<citation rid="R3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24703084" doi="10.1016/j.gie.2013.10.039" count="1">3</citation>] <sentence_start/>In general, gastroenterologists hope to efficiently identify and treat a bleeding site by investing only one or few endoscopic procedures. <sentence_start/>Occasionally, however, a patient may undergo multiple consecutive endoscopic procedures to diagnose the cause of bleeding and achieve hemostasis. <sentence_start/>A variety of circumstances contribute to sequences involving multiple endoscopic procedures. [<citation rid="R4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20801285" doi="10.1016/j.gie.2010.04.032" count="1">4</citation>-<citation rid="R6" ref-type="bibr" pmcid="PMC2886381" pmid="20567529" count="1">6</citation>] <sentence_start/>Lesions that bleed only intermittently are sometimes difficult to detect. <sentence_start/>Large amounts of blood inside the visceral lumen or an overlying blood clot compromise the diagnosis and treatment of a bleeding lesion. <sentence_start/>In a patient who harbors more than one potential bleeding site, the initially diagnosed lesion may not represent the true culprit for the patient’s GIB. <sentence_start/>The bleeding site resides outside the reach of the initial endoscope and a different type of instrumentation is needed to diagnose or treat the GIB. <sentence_start/>Repeat endoscopy is also required if hemostasis is not achieved during the initial endoscopy or if the bleeding restarts few days later after achieving initial hemostasis. <sentence_start/>Other potential causes for lengthy sequences involving repeat endoscopy abound, but the medical literature contains little if any information about the number of endoscopies and length of workup to be expected in the average management of GIB. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, the aims of the present observational study were to examine the length of GIB workup with respect to the number of procedures and time, and to examine the consecutive utilization of different endoscopic procedures based on the initial bleeding presentation.
note: Same hyphen-range-citation mistake as the PMC1685661 entry above ('[1-3]' and '[4-6]' both split mid-bracket), a different concrete instance -- this one article alone has 5 occurrences of the pattern, only 2 included here.
